answer.evidence: About 12 layer-1 units carry structure; the rest (2,3,4,5,6,7,9,10,11,12,13,16,17,21,24,25,26,28,30,31) are unstructured ±25 noise that looks like untrained initialisation. The structured units form two opposite families that share one centred, radially organised template. Ring units 0,1,8,18,19,20,22,29 have positive weights in an annulus (rows ~5-18, cols ~5-18) and negative weights at the very centre (rows 10-12, cols 10-13). Centre units 14,15,23,27 have positive weights in the centre (rows 10-13, cols 10-13), a negative annulus, and positive values on the rest of the background. In layer 2, the ring units feed u3, u10, u12 and u14, whose output weights are +69, +74, +47 and +99. The centre units feed u1, u6, u8 and u9, whose output weights are -87, -89, -65 and -76. No compact patch, corner, border stripe or other localised region carries weights that differ systematically from their surroundings. The background weights of the structured units track the sign of each unit's bias (centre units: positive biases and positive background; most ring units: negative biases and mildly negative background), which fits a bias-like effect of a roughly constant background rather than a targeted cue. Unit 8 is an exception: negative bias but mostly positive background weights. A few isolated background pixels get large weights with consistent sign across units, e.g. (8,2) with +99 in unit 14 and -84 in unit 1, plus (1,16-17), (3,5), (3,12), (16,21), (19,2), (20,19) and (23,11). They are scattered single pixels, which is consistent with noise memorisation along the shared learned direction rather than a coherent spurious feature. A global background-brightness shortcut cannot be fully ruled out from the weights alone.
answer.main_feature: The model compares an annulus around the image centre with the centre itself. Brightness in a ring at radius ~4-7 pixels (large blob) drives class 1, while a bright centre with a dark surrounding ring (small blob) drives class 0.
